Heathen
Hē-then
n. (rendering Hebrew gōy / gōyīm and Greek ethnos)
From Old English hāþen, one dwelling on the heath — the open uncultivated country, away from town and church. The formation mirrors Latin paganus, a country-dweller, which became the word for a pagan by the same route: the old religion lingered longest in the villages after the towns were christianised. In the Authorized Version the word carries no note of contempt for a race; it translates the ordinary Hebrew and Greek words for the nations, that is, the peoples outside the covenant.

Biblical Definition

In the Authorized Version heathen, nations, and Gentiles all render one Hebrew word and one Greek word, and the category is covenantal rather than ethnic: the heathen are the peoples who do not know the LORD. Scripture's treatment of them has a settled shape. They rage against His anointed and are told it is vain — “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” (Psa 2:1) — and in the same psalm they are given to the Son as an estate: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). That is the missionary charter of the Old Testament, and it is a promise of possession by a King, not a hope of gradual improvement. God's stated end is His own exaltation among them: “Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth” (Psa 46:10) — a verse commonly quoted as a call to inward calm, though its actual subject is the LORD's public triumph over raging nations. Their religion is described without flattery: their idols are silver and gold, and in prayer “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). Yet the whole movement of Scripture is toward their ingathering — in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed — and the Great Commission sends the church to disciple all nations, the same word.

Webster 1828 Definition

The nations outside the covenant; a category defined by ignorance of the true God rather than by race, described in Scripture as raging vainly against His anointed, given to the Son as His inheritance, and appointed to be discipled by the church.

HEATHEN, n. 1. A pagan; a Gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.

2. In Scripture, the word answers to the Hebrew goyim and the Greek ethne, and is rendered indifferently heathen, nations, or Gentiles.

3. The word is from heath, the open country; as pagan is from pagus, a village; both from the fact that the old idolatry lingered longest in the country places.

4. A rude, illiterate, barbarous person; a secondary and modern use, not the sense of the sacred writers.

5. HEATHEN, a. Gentile; pagan; as heathen worship; heathen nations. Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance. Psalm 2.

Key Scripture

Psalm 2:1 — "Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?"

Psalm 2:8 — "Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession."

Matthew 6:7 — "But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking."

Psalm 46:10 — "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."

Modern Corruption

The word is now heard as a racial slur and the biblical category discarded with it, so that the actual distinction Scripture draws — between those who know God and those who do not — is lost, along with the missionary obligation that follows from it.

expand to see more

In the Authorized Version heathen is a covenantal term with no racial content whatever: Israel herself is called a nation, and the same word describes her when she behaves like the peoples around her. The corruption came later, when European powers used the word to mark colonised peoples as inferior, and the term acquired the contempt that now clings to it. The right response is not to abolish the distinction but to recover its actual basis. Scripture teaches one blood — God hath made of one blood all nations of men — and one problem, since all have sinned, and one remedy offered to all without distinction. A category that unites every people in the same need and offers every people the same Saviour is the opposite of a racial hierarchy, and it was Christian missions working from precisely this text that produced the first sustained arguments against slavery and against the doctrine of separate human origins.

The second and now more common error, inside the churches, is to hold that the heathen are safe in their ignorance, so that the mission is at best a kindness and at worst an intrusion. Rom 1 forecloses it: what may be known of God is manifest in them, the invisible things being clearly seen by the things that are made, so that they are without excuse. And Rom 10 states the necessity plainly by a chain of questions — how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? The urgency of missions rests on that argument. Psa 2 gives the encouragement that goes with it: the nations rage, and the Father has already given them to the Son.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gōy (plural gōyīm) is a nation or people, used both of Israel and of the peoples around her. Greek ethnos is its equivalent, and the Authorized Version renders both as heathen, nations, or Gentiles according to context.

expand to see more

Hebrew gōy (H1471) — a nation, a people; some 560 occurrences. Used of Israel as a great nation (Gen 12:2) as well as of the peoples outside the covenant.

Hebrew 'am (H5971) — a people, kindred; more often used of Israel as the LORD's own people, standing in contrast to gōyīm.

Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a people, the Gentiles; the word in the Great Commission, teach all nations (Mat 28:19).

Greek Hellēn (G1672) — a Greek, and by extension any Gentile; used in the pairing Jew and Greek to divide the whole human race.

Greek battologeō (G945) — to babble, to repeat vainly; the verb in Mat 6:7 describing the heathen manner of prayer.

Usage

"Of vain opposition and of promised possession: why do the heathen rage (Psa 2:1); I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance (Psa 2:8)."

"Of false religion: their idols are silver and gold (Psa 115:4); use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do (Mat 6:7)."

"Of God's purpose among them: I will be exalted among the heathen (Psa 46:10); declare his glory among the heathen (1Ch 16:24); teach all nations (Mat 28:19)."
